speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my words of appreciation to those of the hon. members who have preceded me in the honours accorded to the members of the armed forces in moving and seconding the address of his excellency in the speech from the throne. I think every member of this house realizes that our armed forces are the spearhead which stands between our democratic way of life and nazism, that the very existence of this house is dependent upon their initiative and their success.
The Address-Mr. Wright

I should like also to compliment the new leader of the Progressive Conservative group (Mr. Graydon) upon the honour which has been accorded him by his associates. I am, however disappointed that he should have accepted even the temporary leadership of a group which for the past seven years has consistently set its sails to catch every political breeze which has been blowing in Canada and then found when the sails were set that the wind had veered and they were again left in the doldrums. I am disappointed also that they should, in stating their mobilization policy, have again used the qualifying phrase. The hon. member should have known by now that he cannot compete with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who has had thirty years experience in this house in the use of that phrase. Their mobilization plank reads:
We believe in the effective total utilization and proper allocation for war, by compulsion where necessary, of all the resources of Canada, including agriculture, industry and finance.
That is exactly the policy of the government. mobilization where necessary. I do not think that is what the people of Canada desire to-day. I believe they desire total mobilization, mobilization of industry and finance on the same basis as we have mobilization of man-power at the present time. I know that is what the people in my part of Saskatchewan believe.
He complained also about the adoption by the government of many of the planks in their platform. This is nothing more than could be expected because there is to-day no fundamental difference between the two major political parties in this country. They both believe in capitalism; they both believe in the return to capitalism immediately this, war is over. The people of Canada realize that to-day there is no fundamental difference. This is not only my opinion; it is the opinion of some of the keenest political observers in Canada. Mr. Grattan O'Leary, writing in Maclean's magazine of December 1. 1942, said this:
Except in labels there has been no difference between the liberal conservatism of the party led by Meighen, Bennett and Manion and the conservative liberalism of the party led by Mackenzie King. If there has been difference at all it has been in that while the Conservatives practised liberalism in office and talked toryism in opposition, the Liberals talked liberalism in opposition and practised conservatism in office. In fundamentals they have been alike as two peas.
But in Canada to-day there are two distinct lines of thought. There are those who believe in the continuation of our present capitalistic system and there are those who believe in a 
cooperative economy. The one is the direct opposite of the other; both cannot continue to exist and expand in any country; one must supersede the other. Capitalism stands for the control of the services and productive facilities of this country by individuals and groups of individuals who shall operate them at a profit for themselves. On the other hand, cooperation 'believes that these services and productive facilities should be owned by the people cooperatively in order that the services may be provided at cost. Any political party or parties that contend that they believe in the return to capitalism and believe in cooperation are patently trying to ride two horses at the same time. The farmers of this country know that is an absolute impossibility.
We hear a good deal of talk about free enterprise under the capitalistic system. Free enterprise is fast disappearing under our present monopolistic capitalistic system. The farmers of Canada are concerned over what is going to take its place. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believe, as do the farmers of this country, that a cooperative economy is the only democratic solution and is the only method by which the individual can use his initiative effectively at the present time. I do not think I need to bring this particularly to the attention of the house. We have seen in many instances during the past thirty years the disappearance of private initiative. To-day the small storekeepers are finding it practically impossible to compete with the chain stores and the mail order houses. The small manufacturer and the small machine-shop have disappeared. The small farmer is disappearing, and the present-day value of farm property has depreciated fifty per cent from what it was twenty years ago. Farms which were worth 110,000 twenty years ago, to-day are worth approximately So,000. This is what has happened under a capitalistic system.
That is why the farmer is now becoming more and more a cooperator, and a believer in the cooperative movement. He believes that lack of planning is hampering production on all farming fronts. His criticism is that he is deprived of any opportunity to participate in the planning of the contribution which he will make. Had the counsel of the farmers been sought, many of these blunders might have been avoided. In the fourth year of the w*ar this government continues to leave economic controls largely in the hands of business men who have been trained in the technique of monopolistic capitalism, while they ignore almost completely the counsel of the farmers. Under such domination there

The Address-Mr. Wright
is great possibility of the enterprise and initiative of the farmer being further endangered and crushed.
Not only have the recommendations of the national federation of agriculture been ignored, but no attention has been paid to the part that could have been played by local committees and by the farmer producer and consumer cooperatives. One of the most glaring results of this lack of planning is the farm labour shortage that we have in Canada today. Last March the Prime Minister stated in a speech in the house that it was the intention of the government to maintain the men then on the farms in their positions there, except those who wished to enlist voluntarily. After that address in the house, the then Minister of National War Services issued a press release explaining the new policy which had been adopted. In explaining the difference between the new policy and the old, he said:
There is, however, this fundamental difference, namely, that if the applicant is a person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture within the meaning of the amended regulations, the board, subject to certain exceptions hereafter mentioned, shall-
The word "shall" is underlined:
-grant him a postponement order until further notice and such postponement order shall be an allocation of such person to agriculture.
It is this direction to the board, namely, that the board shall grant him a postponement order until further notice, that constitutes the "fundamental alteration of the policy regarding compulsory military training and service where such service touches persons wholly or mainly employed in agriculture," referred to by the Prime Minister in his speech in the House of Commons on Tuesday, March 24, 1942.
Previously, under subsections (1) and (2) of section 14 of the national war services regulations, it was provided that the board "shall have power to grant an advancement or postponement order when it is of the opinion that it is in the national interest to do so," but there was no obligation upon the board to grant such orders. The matter was left to the discretion of the boards.
There has therefore been a fundamental change of base in the regulations. It is not a question of greater latitude having been given to the boards in the matter of granting postponement orders. Nor is it a matter of preferential treatment. The amendments go much further and constitute a fundamental change of approach, both by the applicant and by the board. When the applicant has shown that he is a person wholly or mainly employed or engaged in agriculture within the meaning of the amended regulations, he is prima facie entitled to a postponement order until further notice. He does not have to prove, as was the ease formerly, a special case for postponement of a fixed duration.
These instructions have certainly not been followed by the mobilization boards in western Canada, at least not by the ones with which 72537-7
I have had contact. As far as the Saskatchewan board is concerned, it has proceeded in exactly the same manner as before. It is calling up men from agriculture and granting them only temporary postponements. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speaking in western Canada a- short time ago, stated that only ten per cent of the men from agriculture applying for postponement to the Saskatchewan board have been refused, but I maintain that that is only a half truth. The whole truth is-

speechtext:
I am not stating that the
minister's information was not correct; what I am stating is that if it is correct, these men were granted postponement for only a short period, and within six months from seventy-five to eighty-five per cent of those who had been granted postponement found themselves in the armed forces. I had an instance brought 'to my attention. A young chap wrote to the board asking for a postponement for three weeks in order that he might complete his arrangements before he was called up. In reply he received a telegram from the board stating that if he would signify his willingness to enlist for active service, there would be no trouble about granting the postponement. These things are not right, and the government must face this problem in a realistic manner. They cannot have at one and the same time both more men in the armed forces and greater production as far as western agriculture is concerned, and I believe this applies to eastern Canada as well. The man-power problem is acute. In substantiation of what I have said I wish to quote a telegram which has just been received by the leader of our group. It is from Rosetown-Biggar and reads:
Am farming two sections and half of land. Am up against it for farm help. My last man just called up. Have over sixty head cattle, over hundred sheep, thirty brood sows, twenty horses and nobody to look after them. I am sick and cannot get help. What am I to do? It would be a great sacrifice to sell stock. Have had four or five men working other years, now the last man is going. Please advise.
If the government requires greater production from western agriculture I believe that the men who are on the farms in western Canada to-day should remain there.
There is another matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the government. In obtaining evidence as to the essentiality of a man to agriculture the practice has grown

The Address-Mr. Wright

up in western Canada of using the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as the body to make a report. I have every confidence in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police when it comes to enforcing the law. I believe they have done wonderful work in Canada during this war in preventing sabotage, but I maintain that they are not the proper body to make these reports. Many of the men who are at present in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in western Canada are young constables, the older men having gone to other posts. These young constables are not acquainted with the people ip the locality in which they are stationed, and they must go to somebody else to get information to complete their reports. I know of many instances in which they have never approached the individual concerned but have taken the word of neighbours and other individuals as to the essentiality of that man to agriculture. Reeves of municipalities, the municipal doctor, the clergy and other representative men in the locality have written in to the board signifying that certain individuals were required on the farms, and yet the report of the mounted police has been accepted in preference to the advice given by these people on the spot, with the result that men have been taken off the farms and called up for military service. I know of several instances in my own constituency where that has happened, as a result of which the father of the boy has had to sell his stock and rent his farm, and that farm is being used to-day for the production of more grain instead of producing things which the government requires much more urgently at this time. Local committees of responsible men who know the people in their own community and their circumstances would be a much better source from which the board could obtain evidence than the reports made by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
There are two specific recommendations which I should like to make with regard tc farm labour. I believe that all men now engaged in agriculture should be continued in their present occupation, and that in cases of emergency, where real need is shown, men might be taken from the armed forces in Canada to supply the deficiency of manpower on the farm. I also believe that the services of conscientious objectors who have experience in agriculture might be used. These conscientious objectors are to be found in some of the camps in large numbers. I do not know what the total number is, but many of them are experienced in agriculture. Farming to-day is a specialized industry, and

farm labour must be experienced. A farmer cannot afford to-day to hire an inexperienced man to run machinery which may cost anywhere from two to five thousand dollars a unit.
What happened with regard to the harvesters' excursion which was run to western Canada last fall? Some four weeks before harvesting started in western Canada the government of Saskatchewan made a survey of conditions throughout the province, and every municipality stated what its needs were with regard to harvest help. The provincial government had that information, and I suppose they passed it along to the proper departments at Ottawa. We were told by the Minister of Agriculture and by others that we must depend in Saskatchewan upon our own help in harvesting the crop. Yet when harvesting was almost half completed the labour situation became so serious that the government decided to send large numbers of men from eastern Canada to the west. These men were largely taken from our universities in the east. These men were anxious to do the job, but they were inexperienced and just could not fill the bill. Within a very short time large numbers of them were back in the towns and cities with blistered hands and sore backs, asking to be returned to eastern Canada. Probably fifty per cent of the men who came out on that excursion performed a useful service, but there were large numbers of them who should never have left eastern Canada. There should have been more selection in the choosing of them.
Another thing that happened in Saskatchewan was this. Our university opened as usual. Students from all over Saskatchewan went into the university, and the second day after they were there, universities in eastern Canada closed and started to send their students to Saskatchewan when our own students were there in the university. Immediately the university authorities or the provincial authorities, I do not know which, became alarmed at the anomaly, and the students were sent home. Many of them were left stranded in Saskatoon and had to telephone to their parents to send them the money to pay their fares home. These are examples of lack of efficient planning.
I believe that if serious conditions are not to develop this fall there must be a greater allotment of machinery to western Canada, The allotment of our farm machinery required for production of grain is twenty-five per cent of the 1940 sales. In the case of many companies I was informed that the 1940 sales were very low, and I do not believe that twenty-five per cent of those sales are going to be sufficient to meet the requirements of western

The Address-Mr. Wright
agriculture this year, especially with regard to certain types of machinery. I believe we shall have to have a larger number of combines. One large combine would have taken the place of approximately twenty of those men who came from eastern Canada. During the last year of the last war wheat was selling in western Canada for $2.25 a bushel and you could purchase a binder there at that time for $2S5. To-day it is worth $385. A seed drill which then cost approximately $250 is to-day worth approximately $400. I believe, and the western farmers believe, that there should be a greater parity between the prices we receive to-day for what we have to sell and the prices we have to pay for the commodities we have to buy. The government's policy of freezing farm prices at levels that obtained between September 15 and October 10, 1941, has, I believe, proven unworkable. In a great many instances it has been necessary to adjust these prices by subsidies. These subsidies in some instances have been paid to the processor of agricultural products. In others they have been paid directly to the farmer, but where they have been paid to the processors it was expected that they would pay a higher price for the product which they were processing.
We in this group do not believe in the principle of subsidies. We believe that the government should appoint commodity boards which wouldi purchase from the farmer the products he has to sell, at cost of production or, if that could not be ascertained easily, at a parity price established on the basis of a period of years in which agriculture has received a proportionate share of the national income. If there were a loss to the government, the commodity board could absorb that loss, and we would not have to set up the bureaucracy which in many instances has been set up in the payment of these subsidies in western Canada. As an example of this I would mention the subsidies paid on the wheat acreage reduction plan. We have in western Canada, according to returns tabled in this house, a list of names of men who were paid for this purpose, and according to that list, there were some six hundred men in the west who were doing this inspection work.

speechtext:
In that particular part of
the province which I represent ninety per cent of these men are political appointees, and they are deliberately mixing business with political propaganda. The farmers of Canada have become disgusted with this method of doing business. We had a grain policy announced last Friday by the Minister of Trade
and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), and I should like to compliment him upon the promptness with which the government's grain policy has been announced this year. I would suggest, however, that it would have been better had he consulted organized agriculture, as represented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, before presenting this policy.
There are some things in the policy with which I do not agree. I believe that the stoppage of payment for storage of grain on the farm is not defensible at this time. The minister gives one reason why the policy was adopted. I submit that there are two other reasons. Statistics show that a considerable amount of storage is not being used in the elevators in western Canada. In many in* stances this is because certain elevator companies have bins which have been available for. say, No. 4 wheat, but a large quantity of grain in that particular district is No. 3 wheat, and when the farmer comes and asks if there is a bin for No. 3 wheat he is told that there is no space available but that they have a No. 4 bin if he is willing to accept No. 4 for his wheat. As a result of that, there has been a great deal of grain held back in the country. There are also a large number of farmers in the west who desire to use their own facilities in the delivering of their grain, and they are holding their grain back until there is room in the pool elevators at their particular point so that they may deliver their grain through their own system. This legislation, stopping the payment of storage, is forcing these men to deliver their grain through other sources than those which they would like to use, and they are delivering grain at a lower grade than they should obtain.
With regard to prices, may I say that they are far below a parity level. There has been a great deal of misunderstanding in this country as to what is meant by parity prices. In the United States they took the period of 1909-1913 as the period in which agriculture in that country enjoyed an approximately equal place in the division of the national income with labour and industry, and they worked out a basis of parity prices on that period. In Canada a great many organizations have accepted the period 1926-1929 as being the basis on which parity prices should be established in this country. I would point out that during those years agricultural income was only one-sixth of the national income, although one-third of the employable males in Canada during that period were engaged in agriculture. As far as we are concerned we are not prepared to accept that basis. We believe that a period should be chosen in which.'
The Address-Mr. Wright

agriculture enjoyed a proportionate share of the national income with the other economic groups.
According to a pamphlet issued by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture there has been only one period in Canadian history in which this has occurred; that is, the years 1915-1919. Agriculture will be satisfied with parity prices established only on a basis that will give it a proportionate share in the national income with other groups. This pamphlet shows that the average income per farm in 1932 in Canada was S198 in cash and kind, and Sill in actual cash. From that time on there has been a substantial improvement. In 1941 the total cash income of the farmers of Canada was $876,500,000. Adding produce consumed on the farm amounting to $172,000,000, we get a total income of about $1,048,500,000. Deducting expenses of $363,000,000, which according to the Rowell-Sirois report is about what the expenses would amount to in that year, we get a total net income of $685,500,000. This figure, however, does not include depreciation or interest on investment. Dividing it by the number of farm units, we find that in 1941 the average income per farm was $914.
At the present time we have available income figures for only the first nine months of 1942. Working them out on a percentage basis, we find that the average net income per farm for 1942 would be about $1,005. On the average farm there are at least three people engaged. This gives an average income of about $335 for those three people.
In spite of these facts, we see articles in the press suggesting that the farmer is not paying his fair share of the income tax. This is an entirely inadequate income at this time, and if the government are to get the increased production necessary for a successful war effort they must give further consideration to the establishment of parity prices for farm products, which are at present entirely out of line with the returns to industry.
Another matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the government in connection with increased farm production is this. In industry, if the government wants increased production of any commodity and it is necessary to have new plant and equipment for the purpose, depreciation allowances are made which enable the industry to write off the cost of that plant in two or three years. This was shown quite clearly yesterday by the leader of this group when he read quotations from the report of the special committee on war expenditures. But when the government ask for increased farm production they make

no allowance for depreciation on the additional equipment that the farmer must buy to get that increased production. This is a distinct preference given to industry.
Again I wish to state, as I did at the beginning of my remarks, that it is only by long-term planning for agriculture that we can hope to obtain much further increase in production. While it may be that the present shortages in butter and dairy products are not entirely the fault of the government, nevertheless they must accept a considerable share of responsibility. I do not like to be one of those who say " I told you so," nevertheless in 1940 I did point out in this house that our export of dairy cattle to the United States had increased thirty-five per cent over that for 1939 and our export of calves to that country had increased by fifty per cent. These were largely dairy calves. Anyone who knows anything about agriculture would know that this increasing shipment of dairy stock out of the country would result in a shortage of dairy products sooner or later. Nevertheless nothing was done about it. At that time the price of butter was entirely out of line with the cost of production, and farmers naturally disposed of a large amount of their dairy stock because of that and of the shortage of labour.
If we are to get the increased production that the government have asked for, we must have long-term agreements with the countries to which we are exporting. It is not enough to have agreements which just run from one year to another. Our agreement with Great Britain should continue at least for the duration of the war and two or three years after, so that agriculture could be assured of a market for its products if our herds are increased as the government is asking at the present time. The methods being followed in the United States in their long-term plan, of establishing local committees of farmers prepared to advise in the carrying out of the AAA programme, have been a means of bringing about great additions over there. It is a democratic way of obtaining the support and the participation of the farmers for any such plan, and I believe it could be used with great advantage in Canada to-day in our war-time production effort.
There are several other matters which 1 should like to bring to the government's attention. Two of them are the implementation of the Veterans' Land Act and the amendments to the Soldier Settlement Board Act recommended by the committee on land settlement last year. In that special committee last year I endeavoured to have a parity' price clause written into that agreement. I thought this might be a suitable place for

The Address-Mr. Hazen
the government to introduce the principle of parity prices in our agricultural economy. Here we have a small group of the most deserving of our citizens who were going to be placed in agriculture on their return to Canada. Surely, if the government was genuine in its protestations of desire to better agricultural conditions, this would be a good point to start. They refused, however, to introduce this amendment. Nevertheless the committee brought in a recommendation that the government give further consideration to the principle of parity prices. I should like to know if the government has given this matter consideration, and, if so, what its decision is.
There was also the matter of the treatment of soldier settlers of the last war. I did not consider that the recommendations made by the committee which dealt with the matter were sufficient, and this year I should like to see the committee reconstituted in order that it might receive a report from Mr. Murchison, director under the new Veterans' Land Act, as to what progress has been made under that act, and so that we might be able to make certain recommendations to him at this time.
There is also the matter of the allowances paid to the girls who are at present in our armed forces. I understand an order in council has been passed' providing that women employed in industry shall receive the same wages as 'the men they are displacing. If this applies to women in industry, I believe it should apply equally to the girls who are going into our armed forces. They are displacing men, taking over their jobs, and I believe they should receive the same pay as the men. That is only fair, and the government should give consideration to this matter. There are also the matters of old age pensions, veterans' widows' allowances, health insurance and the social security provisions, on which I hope to have more to say at a later date.
There was, however, one matter taken up in the speech from the throne, on which I should like to say something definite at this time. I refer to the question of redistribution. Under the new act we in Saskatchewan will lose four members, and I believe Manitoba will lose three. We believe that any redistribution at this time is going to work an injustice as far as Saskatchewan is concerned. Large numbers of men and women who formerly lived in that province have gone elsewhere to secure employment. Many families from the south of the province were settled in the north, in the reestablishment areas, where their living was very slim indeed. As soon as war broke out and employment became
available in other parts of the dominion, these people came east or went to the coast, where at present they are employed in war industry. There is no doubt that immediately the war ends, many of those people will return to Saskatchewan. If to-day under any redistribution bill the numbeT of seats in Saskatchewan is reduced, two years from now, when those people return to Saskatchewan and our population again increases, as I believe it will, we shall not be fairly represented in this house; and that will apply for the next ten years. Consideration should be given this point in any redistribution carried out at this time. I also believe that instead of a committee of the house we should set up a commission to deal with this matter. Redistribution has been a political football too long. I believe We will get a fairer redistribution through a commission than through a committee of this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to ask the government if it approves the "don't give a damn for the middleman" policy that has been adopted by the wartime prices and trade board. I do not ask this question in any spirit of levity; I ask it in all seriousness, because I have been informed by businessmen from my own community, on their return from Ottawa where they had been discussing with the board difficult problems which confronted them, that the officers of that board had told them in no uncertain terms that they "did not give a damn for the middleman."
I found it hard to believe that such a policy had been adopted by the board, but a short time ago, at a public meeting in the city hall of Saint John, called by the mayor of that city, to inquire into certain difficulties regarding the delivery of milk which had arisen by reason of regulations recently passed by the New Brunswick dairy products commission, the secretary of that commission told the meeting that recently he had been in Ottawa and said, I quote his remarks from the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of January 14:
The wartime prices and trade board is interested in the price to the consumer and the price to the producer; as far as the middleman is concerned, the wartime prices and trade board does not give a damn; he has to stand the squeeze.
A policy that does not give a damn for the middleman or for the little man, a policy that squeezes him out of business, cannot, in my opinion, be justified. Under our system
The Address-Mr. Iiazen

of competitive business and freedom of enterprise, he carries on because he renders a service to the community. To adopt a policy of "don't give a damn" toward him and to make regulations that will squeeze him out of business is to adopt a policy which at the conclusion of this war, or perhaps before that time, will place all the business of this country in the hands of great corporations and monopolies.

speechtext:
Not just now, if you please.
I know that the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or socialist party, in a radio address only a few evenings ago, said:
. . . when peace comes there must be no return to the old way of doing business with its unplanned, unregulated competition. . . .
1 do not agree with that statement. In my opinion, competition subject to proper safeguards as to hours of labour and living standards of wages, is the life of trade and of economic progress; and only as long as we have freedom of competition and freedom of enterprise will freedom continue to exist in this country.
I was not inclined to believe that the government would approve any such unwise and dangerous policy, but only a few days ago I read an address given in Vancouver by Mr. Donald Gordon, the energetic and able chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, during the course of which he said:
In spite of uninformed critics, responsible government was nowhere more in evidence than in the administration of the board. The suggestion that the board or its chairman could wield wide powers without ministerial control or responsibility was not in accordance with the facts.
If the correct conclusion to be drawn from that statement is that the government approves this don't-give-a-damn policy, then I have no hesitation in saying that it is time it reconsidered that policy, and came to some other decision in the matter. I would say further that the time has come when these regulations, or some of them, should be reviewed, and, when necessary, altered in order to protect the middleman and the small businessman.
This matter was forcibly brought to my attention recently by certain regulations that were passed by the New Brunswick dairy products commission. This commission was established by act of the New Brunswick legislature in 1935. Its object was declared to be, and I quote from the act:

The enforcement of commercial ethics and marketing conditions that will enure to the common benefit of the dairy trade and the general public.
The dairy trade, the act states, comprises the producer-suppliers, or farmers, the vendors, the dealers or dairies and the storekeepers.
The vendors are the men who buy their milk from the dairies and sell it to their customers who, until these regulations came into force, were stores, restaurants, hotels, institutions and private homes.
Most of these dealers, or dairies, in addition to selling milk to the vendors also have their own delivery wagons, and sold milk to the householders.
These vendors had been in business for many years in the city of Saint John. They would be up every morning, about half past two, and would reach the dairies at a very early hour. They would have their milk delivered to their customers in time for breakfast. They would not finish their work until some time in the afternoon. Their hours were long and the work was hard. But these men did not think the country owed them a living, and they did not look for government bonuses or assistance. They made their living by rendering a service to the community.
Recently, without consultation with the dairies, without consultation with the vendors, without taking any expert advice so far as I have been able to find out-and I questioned the commission about it-the commission issued certain regulations having the force of law, which provided that in future all milk sold to stores, hotels or other institutions had to be sold by the dairies themselves, and could not be sold by the vendors. These regulations took from the vendors about fifty per cent of their business-the best part of it, because it is much easier to deliver two or three cases of milk to a store, hotel or some other institution than to climb up one or two flights of stairs to deliver one or two bottles of milk to one householder and one or two to another. Not only did it take away about half of their business, and the better half, but it cut their incomes in half. It did all this without providing them with any compensation whatsoever.
Undoubtedly it was highly pleasing to the dairies, or most of them., to get the best part of the vendors' business, without any expense to themselves. But it worked a great hardship and a great injustice to the vendors; for these men had families to keep, rent to pay, taxes, insurance premiums and other obligations to meet, and this drastic cut in

The Address-Mr. Hazen
their income put them right on the spot. They had no redress other than to appeal to public opinion.
In effect the commission said to these men, "Sell your trucks to the dairies; get jobs with them as hired1 men, or else be content to get along with half of what you are earning now, or seek some other form of employment".
This, sir, is Hitlerism with a vengeance. It is a step toward the establishment of a totalitarian state in the place of freedom of enterprise in competitive business.
If three or four persons get together, break into my house and steal my property we call them gangsters and thieves, but three or four people can get together and take away half of the business of certain hard-working taxpayers in a community, and we call them a commission. It would be just as well if we called, a spade a spade. It would be well- and I think the time has come-to take steps to put a stop to such wrong-doing.
Not all the dairies of Saint John were pleased to get this business. One of them, which had been established by a man who had a thorough knowledge of the dairy business, first as a farmer or producer, and then as a vendor, conducted its business on a different system. It did not make any of its own deliveries. All of its milk was delivered by vendors.
Many dairies which made their own deliveries had had a difficult time of it. Some of them failed. But this particular dairy went ahead. The system had great advantages. Under it the vendors owned their own delivery wagons, and consequently took a greater interest in and greater care of them than hired employees would have done. The vendors were interested in getting additional customers, and this meant more business for the dairy. The vendors made their own collections, thereby making fewer bad debts, and the sydtem resulted in a simpler and cheaper method of accounting for this dairy.
Under the new regulation, if this particular dairy were to remain in business it had to buy additional	trucks at a	time when	it wasdifficult, if not indeed impossible, to obtain them.	It	had1 to hire	additional	men todeliver	its milk at a	time when	it wasdifficult, if not impossible, to hire competent men.	It	had to set	up a much more
elaborate system of bookkeeping in its office. There was arbitrary interference with business management. It completely upset the system under which this dairy had successfully conducted its business, and the managing director of the firm had grave doubts if it would be possible for him to carry on successfully if these regulations were enforced.
Among other things, the regulations provided that all milk and cream had to be delivered in a conveyance owned by the dairy and operated by a full-time employee. This meant that no dairy could hire a vehicle or a man part-time to make deliveries. The effect of this regulation is that if I own a truck or other conveyance which I do not use all the time and wish to get some additional revenue from it and a dairy would like to hire it from me, I cannot rent it to the dairy nor can I get employment with the dairy for parttime. This is restriction of individual rights that goes to the extreme.
The chairman of the commission said in a statement which appeared in, the press on January 4 last that these regulations had been passed "to eliminate duplication and overlapping." As a matter of fact the regulations do not prevent duplication and overlapping. There were just as many trucks delivering milk on the streets of Saint John after the regulations were passed as there were before. They did prevent vendors from delivering milk to stores, hotels, restaurants and other institutions, but they did not prevent them from driving up to a store or restaurant, stopping their trucks, walking upstairs and delivering milk to customers who might live above the store or the restaurant.
The reason given by the commission convinced no one, and the public are up in arms over the injustice that has been done to the vendors who are hard working men,, some of whom served in the last war and some of whom have sons serving in this war.
When the public began to take an active interest in the controversy because of the injustice that had1 been done, the commission announced that these regulations had the approval of the wartime prices and trade board. I do not know the details of the communications that passed between the commission and the board; I have not been informed of any of the details of the conversations that took place between them, but I have good reason to believe that the board1 was not fully apprised of the situation, although it should have been. I doubt very much if it would have given, these regulations its approval had it known, that the vendors' business was being taken away from them without compensation and handed over to the dairies as a free gift.
May I give brief details of one or two instances of the effect of these regulations upon the vendors. A man owned a small dairy farm about two miles by road from Saint John. He became a vendor with five customers. These customers were one or two of the largest hotels and two or three of the largest restaurants, all centred about one public
The Address-Mr. Hazen

square. When the regulations came into force he went to the commission and asked them if he could deliver his milk by horse and wagon, assuming that the regulations had been passed to save gasoline and rubber. He was told that he could not, but there was nothing to prevent him from loading his motor vehicle up with milk at his farm and driving several miles past the centre of the city to sell his milk at wholesale to some of the dairies who would then pasteurize it and get an additional price and an additional profit when they delivered it.
In another instance a vendor had not been very successful. He was forced to sell his truck and what customers he had to a dairy and get a job as a hired man with it. The dairy then gave three * vendors who purchased milk from it about thirty'' quarts each. This was milk which this man used to sell to householders. But it took away from them over 200 quarts of milk each which they used to sell to stores or restaurants, and it said to them, "If you keep on selling to stores or restaurants we will not sell you any milk at all."
I can readily understand that a system of zoning in the distribution of milk might save duplication and overlapping in large communities, but I am not in a position to say whether a zoning system would be practicable or would effect any worth-while saving in Saint John. These regulations, however, did not establish a zoning system. If they are intended to be the first step toward a zoning system, it has been a very ill-advised step, a step that cannot be justified. If it is proposed to establish a zoning system, the steps taken to set it up should be based upon the foundation of fair play and justice and not upon confiscation without compensation.
In bringing this matter before the house, I do not want to be misunderstood1. I am not making an attack upon the wage stabilization and price-ceiling policy of the government. I believe that all reasonable efforts should be made to keep inflation under control. I agree with what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said yesterday, that there is an obligation upon every member of this house to help to interpret the necessary restrictions that further our war effort, particularly those restrictions which some people find to be irksome or irritating. But I say that neither fear of inflation nor the furtherance of our war effort should lead the government to approve injustices such as taking people's businesses away from them without compensation and making a free gift of it to other companies or corporations.

These regulations which have been approved by the *wartime prices and trade board are most unjust. They serve no useful purpose and I would ask the government to instruct the wartime prices and trade board to review the situation with a view to withdrawing the approval which it has given, or else to insist that the vendors be fully compensated for the business which has been taken away from them.
This is not the first time I have complained in this house about citizens having been deprived of their rights without compensation. I have on more than one occasion protested against the regulation that was passed on the recommendation of the then Minister of Fisheries, which deprived the owners of property fronting on the non-tidal waters of the Saint John river of their proprietary rights in fisheries. I do not propose to deal with that matter now, but it is an injustice that must in the end be rectified.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say what perhaps I should have said when I began. I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Harris) and the seconder (Mr. Halle) of the address upon the excellent speeches they made. It was most fitting and proper that members of the armed forces, one an English-speaking Canadian from the province of Ontario and the other a French-speaking Canadian from the province of Quebec, one who had been overseas and expects soon to return overseas, and the other who expects to take his unit overseas within a very short time, should have moved and seconded the address. The speeches they made were the speeches of loyal British subjects and of loyal Canadians who realized the very serious situation which we face to-day, and I have much pleasure in congratulating both of them upon what they said on Friday afternoon.
On motion of Mr. Gershaw the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre) the house adjourned at 10.58 p.m.
